_meta.what: The labour-extraction evidence file: how India's urban working classes are extracted from in the BUILDING and the RUNNING of cities. Sections: construction_migrant, bocw_cess, contractor_chain, road_contracts, gig_platform, reproduction_extraction, caste_composition. Each section is an array of claim-objects: {claim, tier, figure, source, verify}. This is the labour underside of the corporate-city atlas: where docs/the-corporate-city.md shows the municipality built to take rent not give service, THIS file shows whose bodies pay for the building and the running.
_meta.thesis: Two frames held together. HARVEY: capital's SECONDARY CIRCUIT is the built environment (real estate, infrastructure) — a sink for surplus that depends on a cheap, disposable, mobile construction proletariat; and ACCUMULATION BY DISPOSSESSION continues in the city through a SECONDARY EXTRACTION in the sphere of reproduction (workers who built the city must then BUY water, rent, sanitation back at predatory prices). AMBEDKAR: the 'division of labour' in caste society is also a 'division of labourers' (Annihilation of Caste) — graded, hereditary, unequal. The urban labour hierarchy is caste-coded top to bottom: construction (OBC/SC/Adivasi/Muslim migrant), sanitation and sewer death (Valmiki/SC), head-loading (Dalit) — graded inequality reproduced as a labour market.

tier_legend.A: DOCUMENTED FACT — official, audit, court, or census figures with named source.
tier_legend.B: REPORTED ALLEGATION — asserted by a named source (NGO/union/journalist/petitioner), attributed not asserted as established fact.
tier_legend.C: ANALYSIS — our interpretive/framing claim, not a primary datum.

_meta.rigor_note: Public repo. No fabrication. Tier-A figures carry official/audit/court/census provenance. Tier-B figures are attributed to a named reporter or organisation and never stated as settled fact. Where a figure is the strongest available but not firmly sourced to a primary document, verify:true. Cess/workforce headcounts are the most solid (Parliament answers, SC orders, ministry estimates); per-incident death tallies and the 'jamadar advance' mechanism are reported/qualitative and tiered accordingly.
_meta.status: Authored 2026-06 from Parliament answers (MoS Labour, Dec 2022), Supreme Court judgments (NCC-CL v UoI 2011/2018), CAG audit reports (UP Contract Management in Road Works 2017; Karnataka; Kerala), Ministry of Labour & Employment estimates, e-Shram portal data, NITI Aayog gig-economy report (2022), state gig-worker statutes (Rajasthan 2023, Karnataka 2025), British Safety Council/Business Standard on construction fatalities, water-tanker reporting (Foreign Policy, water-alternatives.org), and the atlas's own contractualization_map.json + manual_scavenging_map.json for the caste/sanitation layer.

construction_migrant.claim: Construction is India's second-largest employer after agriculture, and overwhelmingly informal/unskilled.
construction_migrant.figure: ~5 crore (50M) construction workers per Ministry of Labour & Employment estimates (2020); industry/other estimates ~7.1 crore (71M) by 2023, projected to cross 10 crore by 2030. ~81% of the workforce is unskilled, ~19% skilled.
construction_migrant.source: Ministry of Labour & Employment (~5 cr, 2020), cited in Construction Week India / Disha Foundation; constructionplacements.com (71M, 2023).

construction_migrant.claim: A large majority of the urban construction workforce is migrant; construction is the single biggest absorber of internal migrant labour.
construction_migrant.figure: An estimated ~50-60% of the construction workforce is migrant; ~15 million migrants are estimated to work in construction.
construction_migrant.source: Migration/construction literature summarised in Anantam IAS, IJCRT 2025; widely cited migrant-labour estimates.

construction_migrant.claim: The workforce is fed by CIRCULAR (seasonal, back-and-forth) migration from a stable set of poor source states.
construction_migrant.figure: Principal sending states: Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh, Rajasthan. ~100 million people are estimated to be in circular migration. 10 UP districts and 6 Bihar districts account for ~25% of male out-migration. Destinations: Delhi-NCR, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala, Punjab.
construction_migrant.source: Census 2011 migration tables; Economic Survey / India Forum 'India's Migrants: Exclusion by Design'; Anantam IAS summary.

construction_migrant.claim: Construction is the deadliest sector in India for workers; site fatalities run to dozens per day, and most go unreported.
construction_migrant.figure: ~38 fatal accidents a day in construction (British Safety Council, cited 2022-23); construction contributes ~24.2% of the ~48,000 estimated annual occupational-accident deaths in India. Karnataka alone records ~75-80 construction-site deaths/year. Reporters and safety bodies note the true toll is higher because most site deaths and delayed-injury deaths are never recorded.
construction_migrant.source: British Safety Council India 'Construction in India: a dangerous business' (2022); Business Standard 'Three deaths every day' (2023); Business & Human Rights Resource Centre (Karnataka).

construction_migrant.claim: The reserve-army dynamic: an oversupplied, mobile, undocumented workforce keeps wages low and discipline cheap — workers are interchangeable and disposable.
construction_migrant.figure: qualitative — the informality (~81% unskilled, no written contracts, circular churn) is itself the mechanism that maintains a reserve army of labour for the secondary circuit (Harvey).
construction_migrant.source: Analysis (Harvey, secondary circuit / industrial reserve army), grounded in the workforce-informality figures above.

bocw_cess.claim: ★ The state collects a statutory welfare cess on construction but leaves a huge share UNSPENT — the single strongest documented case in this file. As of Nov 2022 state welfare boards held tens of thousands of crore unused.
bocw_cess.figure: State BOCW Welfare Boards had collected Rs 87,478.79 crore in cess and spent Rs 49,269.20 crore as on 1 Nov 2022 — leaving Rs 38,209.59 crore UNSPENT (~44%). Stated to Parliament by the Minister of State for Labour & Employment (Rameswar Teli).
bocw_cess.source: MoS Labour answer to Parliament, Dec 2022, reported by ETV Bharat 'Building, other construction workers boards have Rs 38,209 cr unused'.

bocw_cess.claim: The unspent problem is long-standing and was documented by the CAG and the Supreme Court years earlier — the proportions barely improved.
bocw_cess.figure: As of ~Oct 2016, states had collected ~Rs 28,455 crore and spent only ~Rs 6,097 crore (~21%) — over Rs 22,000 crore unspent. By Feb 2022, ~Rs 78,521 crore collected with 54.91% unutilised.
bocw_cess.source: Factly 'Shortchange: construction workers' cess'; Deccan Herald 'States collected Rs 78,521 crore... 54.91% remains unutilised'.

bocw_cess.claim: The Supreme Court has repeatedly strictured the state over the unspent cess in National Campaign Committee for Central Legislation on Construction Labour (NCC-CL) v. Union of India.
bocw_cess.figure: In NCC-CL v UoI (WP(C) 318/2006), the Court recorded that >Rs 37,400 crore had been collected under the Cess Act but only ~Rs 9,500 crore utilised; called the facts 'startling'; directed (19 Mar 2018) a model welfare scheme, social audits by states/UTs of BOCW Act implementation, and that the cess be put to gainful use.
bocw_cess.source: Supreme Court, NCC-CL v Union of India, judgment 19 March 2018 (indiankanoon.org/doc/71520761); Law Times Journal case note.

bocw_cess.claim: Where the cess IS spent, it is sometimes DIVERTED away from workers; the unspent balance is blamed on workers' non-registration — i.e. the state under-registers the very workers it taxes for.
bocw_cess.figure: CAG found Rs 416.33 crore from MP's Construction Workers' Welfare Fund diverted to populist schemes. Maharashtra's board had Rs 11,794 cr of which 73.02% (Rs 8,612.33 cr) unspent, attributed to low worker registration. MP board unspent balance Rs 1,959.63 cr as on 31 Mar 2022.
bocw_cess.source: CAG Report (MP), via The Wire 'Rs 416.33 Cr... Diverted to Populist Schemes'; Karnataka BWWB analysis (Maharashtra/MP figures).

bocw_cess.claim: Kerala is the documented positive outlier — the one board spending the large majority of what it collects.
bocw_cess.figure: Only ~13 States/UTs had spent more than a third of cess funds; only Kerala's welfare board had spent more than 90% of cess collected.

contractor_chain.claim: Recruitment and wage-payment run through a chain of intermediaries (contractor -> petty/sub-contractor -> jamadar/sardar/maistry), each taking a cut — the classic wage-diluting sub-contracting pyramid.
contractor_chain.figure: qualitative chain: principal employer -> labour contractor -> 'jamadar' who recruits whole families from villages; the jamadar is given money for workers' food/clothing/shelter and returns only part to the company, leaving little for the labourer. In brick kilns the equivalent 'sardar' recruits against monetary advances and transports workers to distant states.
contractor_chain.source: Global Annal 'Bonded labor... in Construction Industry'; Journal of Migration Affairs (Bolangir, Odisha brick-kiln sardar system).

contractor_chain.claim: The advance system creates debt-bondage: a wage advance at recruitment ties the worker (and family) to the contractor until repaid through labour, suppressing exit and bargaining.
contractor_chain.figure: qualitative — migrants 'recruited against monetary advances' by sardars/jamadars, repaid through bonded seasonal labour of >6 months under distress conditions; bonded labour documented as persisting in the high-growth construction industry.
contractor_chain.source: Journal of Migration Affairs 'Constrained Subjectivity' (Bolangir); Wikipedia 'Debt bondage in India'; Global Annal.

contractor_chain.claim: Most construction workers have NO written contract, which severs liability and makes minimum-wage, BOCW-registration and accident-compensation enforcement near-impossible.
contractor_chain.figure: qualitative — informality (~81% unskilled, casual, undocumented; only ~12.2% of e-Shram's registered informal workers are in construction despite being ~50M strong) is the documented backdrop; the absence of written contracts is the mechanism that pushes liability down the chain and out of reach.
contractor_chain.source: Analysis grounded in e-Shram sectoral data and Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act 1970 enforcement literature.

contractor_chain.claim: Sub-contracting dilutes the wage and dissolves the legal employer — each tier of the pyramid extracts a margin and disclaims responsibility for wages, safety and statutory dues.
contractor_chain.figure: qualitative — the same dynamic the atlas documents in municipal sanitation (contractualization_map.json): a permanent/secure tier above a precarious sub-contracted tier doing identical work for sub-half wages. In construction the pyramid is deeper and the bottom tier migrant + caste-marked.
contractor_chain.source: Analysis; cross-ref contractualization_map.json wage-gap evidence (Mumbai Rs 24,000 permanent vs Rs 14,500 contract).

road_contracts.claim: CAG audits document systemic irregularities at every stage of road-works contracting — design, estimation, tendering, execution and quality control — across states.
road_contracts.figure: CAG: basic norms for road design and cost estimation not adhered to; tendering lacked transparency and competition; contractors not meeting minimum technical requirements were qualified; 'clear indications of collusive bidding in major contracts in most districts'; 'grant of concessions and undue benefits to contractors was rampant.'
road_contracts.source: CAG, 'Contract Management in Road Works', Government of Uttar Pradesh, Report No. 4 of 2017 (cag.gov.in).

road_contracts.claim: Huge sums flow through road works while quality fails well before design life — the 'pothole economy' of build-fail-rebuild.
road_contracts.figure: UP CAG audit: ~Rs 40,000 crore spent on road works 2011-2016, yet tendering/execution irregularities meant many projects needed repair well before design life. Kerala audit (2020): 85 of 92 tested road projects had no mandatory field labs and no proper job-mix formulas, yet were passed as satisfactory.
road_contracts.source: CAG UP Report No. 4 of 2017; Kerala CAG audit 2020 (via BigStory 'Why India's Roads Crack').

road_contracts.claim: The contractor-engineer nexus: supervising engineers skip or pre-announce inspections; private audit agencies certify substandard works to clear bills; contractors are not blacklisted despite defect-liability breaches.
road_contracts.figure: qualitative — engineers 'skip site visits or pre-announce inspections, giving contractors time to prepare showcase samples'; private audit agencies under scrutiny for clearing substandard road works for bill payment; 'not a single contractor blacklisted for shoddy road works despite gross violations of defect liability clauses.'
road_contracts.source: BigStory 'Why India's Roads Crack Weeks After Opening'; Free Press Journal (Mira-Bhayandar roads); Citizen Matters (Karnataka highway CAG audit).

road_contracts.claim: The corporator-contractor link: the same political economy (re-tendering, repeat repairs, unblacklisted firms) makes potholes a recurring revenue stream rather than a failure to be fixed.
road_contracts.figure: qualitative — read with Ghosh's corporate-city frame (docs/the-corporate-city.md): a road that must be repaired every monsoon is not a malfunction but a contract that renews. The build-fail-rebuild cycle converts a public good into a recurring rent for the contractor-engineer-corporator chain.

gig_platform.claim: Platform/gig work is the new contractor layer running the city's last-mile delivery and mobility; the workforce is large and growing fast.
gig_platform.figure: NITI Aayog: ~77 lakh (7.7 million) gig/platform workers in 2020-21, projected to reach 2.35 crore (23.5 million) by 2029-30. Platforms include Zomato, Swiggy, Uber, Ola, Urban Company, Blinkit/Zepto.
gig_platform.source: NITI Aayog, 'India's Booming Gig and Platform Economy' (2022); PRS / Vidhi summaries.

gig_platform.claim: Rajasthan was the FIRST state to legislate gig-worker welfare, funded by a transaction-based cess on aggregators.
gig_platform.figure: Rajasthan Platform-Based Gig Workers (Registration and Welfare) Act, 2023 (passed July 2023): mandatory registration of workers and aggregators, a unique worker ID portable across platforms, and a 'Platform-Based Gig Workers Welfare Cess' — a percentage of each platform transaction paid into a welfare fund.
gig_platform.source: Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas 'Rajasthan passes... Act, 2023'; The Leaflet; Vidhi Legal Policy comments.

gig_platform.claim: Karnataka followed with its own gig-worker welfare law setting a 1-5% per-transaction welfare fee.
gig_platform.figure: Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Act (passed Aug 2025): welfare fee of 1% to 5% of each gig-worker/platform transaction, by aggregator category, into a welfare fund. Telangana published a draft bill (2025).
gig_platform.source: PRS India (Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers Bill 2025); LabourReview 'Beyond Welfare'.

gig_platform.claim: The core dispute is CLASSIFICATION: platforms treat workers as 'independent partners' not employees, denying minimum wage, hours protection, and accident liability while exercising algorithmic control.
gig_platform.figure: qualitative — the welfare-cess statutes provide a fund but largely sidestep the employee/contractor classification question; the worker remains a 'partner' bearing fuel, vehicle, and risk costs. This is the contractor chain digitised: the algorithm is the new jamadar.
gig_platform.source: Analysis; LabourReview 'Beyond Welfare in India's Gig Sector'; Vidhi comments on the Rajasthan Act.

reproduction_extraction.claim: ★ SECONDARY EXTRACTION (Harvey): the urban poor who BUILD and CLEAN the city must then BUY water back from tanker operators at predatory, per-pot prices — paying many times the municipal rate.
reproduction_extraction.figure: In Mumbai's informal settlements (2012), the median price for tanker water was ~Rs 135 per 1,000 litres — more than 40x the standard municipal charge paid in notified slums and more than 30x the charge paid by other residents. Non-notified slum dwellers can pay as much as Rs 1 per 5 litres — ~50x wealthier areas' rate. Many access <20 litres/person/day, often faecally contaminated.
reproduction_extraction.source: water-alternatives.org Vol 7(1) (Mumbai right-to-water study); NCBI 'The right to water in the slums of Mumbai'; Foreign Policy 'At the Mercy of the Water Mafia' (Delhi).

reproduction_extraction.claim: Tanker 'mafias' operate by siphoning the municipal network and illicit boreholes, then reselling to unauthorised settlements the state declines to pipe — predatory pricing enabled by deliberate non-service.
reproduction_extraction.figure: qualitative — in Delhi, an association of tanker operators sources water from illicit boreholes and by siphoning the city pipe network, selling directly to residents of informal/'unauthorised' colonies; exploitation persists because of poor governance and the settlements' non-notified status.
reproduction_extraction.source: Foreign Policy (Delhi tanker gangs); India Crime 'Water Mafia of Mumbai'; Borgen Project 'Indian Water Mafia'.

reproduction_extraction.claim: Other reproduction-sphere extractions stack on top: informal rents to slumlords, user fees, and moneylender debt — the worker is extracted from again in consumption after being extracted from in production.
reproduction_extraction.figure: qualitative — the same household pays a labour-chain margin (jamadar advance/debt) in production AND a water/rent/credit premium in reproduction. This is accumulation by dispossession operating through the everyday costs of urban survival.
reproduction_extraction.source: Analysis (Harvey, accumulation by dispossession / secondary circuit), grounded in the water-pricing evidence above.

caste_composition.claim: India's informal/unorganised workforce — the labour pool that builds and runs cities — is overwhelmingly SC/ST/OBC and Muslim.
caste_composition.figure: e-Shram portal (>7.86 crore registrations): ~40.5% OBC, ~23.7% SC, ~8.3% ST (~72.5% SC/ST/OBC), ~27.4% general. Construction is the 2nd-largest registered sector (~12.2%) after agriculture (~53.6%).
caste_composition.source: e-Shram portal data, Ministry of Labour & Employment, via Toppersnotes / GKToday '70% informal workers SC, ST, OBCs'.

caste_composition.claim: Sanitation/conservancy work is overwhelmingly Dalit — the floor of Ambedkar's graded division of labourers.
caste_composition.figure: NAMASTE profiling of ~38,000 sanitation workers: 68.9% SC, 14.7% OBC, 8.3% ST (~77% Dalit, ~92% SC/ST/OBC). Manual scavengers ~97% SC (govt data); 2011 census ~95% of ~1.3M scavengers SC. Predominant jati: Valmiki/Balmiki.
caste_composition.source: NAMASTE / Socio-Economic profiling via The News Minute (2024); reused from data/institutions/contractualization_map.json caste_dimension_global.

caste_composition.claim: Sewer/septic-tank cleaning deaths fall almost entirely on the contract/informal Dalit layer — the sharpest expression of caste-coded extraction.
caste_composition.figure: Official (NCSK/Min. Social Justice): 1,313 sewer/septic deaths 1993-2025; 377 in 'hazardous cleaning' 2019-2023. Independent (Safai Karmachari Andolan / Bezwada Wilson): 116 deaths in 2024, 121 in 2025 — roughly double the official count. The dead are almost never permanent mixed-caste staff; they are contract/informal Dalit men.
caste_composition.source: data.gov.in / NCSK; SKA via Maktoob/Deccan Chronicle; reused from data/institutions/manual_scavenging_map.json national_deaths.

caste_composition.claim: The construction migrant tier is OBC/SC/Adivasi/Muslim from the poorest source states — caste and region overlap as a single extractive geography.
caste_composition.figure: qualitative — the source-state set (Bihar/UP/Odisha/Jharkhand/Bengal/Chhattisgarh) maps onto India's most caste-stratified, lowest-wage agrarian regions; circular migration moves caste-disadvantaged labour into the city's secondary circuit, then returns it. e-Shram's ~72.5% SC/ST/OBC share is the documented backdrop.
caste_composition.source: Analysis (Ambedkar, division of labourers; Harvey, secondary circuit), grounded in e-Shram caste data and Census 2011 migration geography.
